# From Module 1

Module 1 confirmed that TPM sums, expression distributions, and PCA structure are reasonable enough to proceed, while flagging that histology is not the only source of variation in the data (PC1 typically explains well under half of total variance in this dataset — see Module 1). With QC complete, this module goes end-to-end: from expression values to a ranked list of **candidate biomarkers**, with an explicit stop along the way to reconnect to the metadata work from Module 0.

**Session plan (≈60 minutes):** presenting the dataset (5 min) → explicit bridge to Module 0 (5 min) → guided walkthrough, Favorable vs Unfavorable (20 min) → adding a real negative control, tumor vs normal (10 min) → light hands-on threshold exploration (10 min) → closing pediatric lens (5 min).

# Part 1 — Presenting the Dataset

Every module so far has used the same real dataset: **TARGET-WT**, RNA-seq expression (TPM) for 124 real pediatric Wilms tumor patients from the Children's Oncology Group's NWTS-5 trial, released through the NCI's **TARGET** program via the **GDC Data Portal**. Samples split into two groups by real clinical histology (`Favorable`, 82 samples, and `Unfavorable`/anaplastic, 42 samples — see Module 0) — not a proxy label, the same grouping used in real clinical risk stratification for this cancer.

<div class="alert-info">
**A note on pediatric-specific resources.** The NCI's **TARGET** program (via the **GDC Data Portal**) is the pediatric-cancer counterpart to the adult-focused **TCGA** — the two share the same portal and file formats, but TARGET covers cancers TCGA does not, including Wilms tumor. This tutorial uses TARGET-WT directly, with the expression matrix and clinical sheet already assembled into `data/` so no live GDC download is needed during the workshop itself (see the README if you want to see how it was built).
</div>

# Part 2 — Explicit Bridge to Module 0

Module 0 built and debugged, by hand, a clinical metadata schema with fields like `patient_id`, `age_years`, `sex`, `diagnosis`, and `consent_status`, then joined the real TARGET-WT expression matrix to a real clinical sheet. Let's look at what metadata actually ships with this real dataset, side by side with that schema.

```{r load-data, echo=TRUE}
# Reload the expression matrix and the verified sample metadata from Module 0.
counts_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/TARGET_WT_gene_expression_tpm.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  rename(gene_symbol = gene_name)

sample_metadata <- read_csv("data/sample_metadata.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

counts_long <- counts_raw %>%
  pivot_longer(-gene_symbol, names_to = "case_submitter_id", values_to = "tpm") %>%
  left_join(sample_metadata, by = "case_submitter_id")
```

```{r table-real-metadata}
datatable(
  sample_metadata,
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel", "pdf"), pageLength = 10),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "The complete real-world metadata available for this dataset: every field TARGET-WT ships with."
)
```

```{r field-comparison}
field_comparison <- tribble(
  ~field,            ~present_in_module0_exercise, ~present_in_target_wt,
  "sample/patient ID", "Yes (patient_id)",           "Yes (case_submitter_id)",
  "group/diagnosis",   "Yes (diagnosis, free text)",  "Yes (histologic_subtype: Favorable/Unfavorable)",
  "age",               "Yes (age_years)",             "Yes (age_at_diagnosis_days)",
  "sex",               "Yes (sex)",                   "Yes (sex_at_birth)",
  "collection date",   "Yes (collection_date)",       "No",
  "consent status",    "Yes (consent_status)",        "No"
)
kable(field_comparison, caption = "Same conceptual fields: TARGET-WT is far closer to the Module 0 schema than a typical public expression dataset.")
```

<div class="alert-info">
**The bridge, stated plainly.** `case_submitter_id` and `histologic_subtype` are literally the same *kind* of information as the `patient_id` and `diagnosis` fields built and debugged by hand in Module 0 — and here, age and sex carry over too, because TARGET is a dedicated, consent-governed pediatric consortium rather than a dataset assembled for a single narrow purpose. It still does **not** ship collection date or a machine-readable consent field via this API — real metadata is rarely complete even from a well-run program, which is exactly why every join is verified rather than trusted, as Module 0 just did.
</div>

# Part 3 — Guided Walkthrough of the Expression Analysis

The rest of this module works through one core question, gene by gene: **"is this gene behaving abnormally compared to what we'd expect?"** Concretely, that means: raw counts → filtering → a statistical comparison between groups → visualization of the result. Each step below states what it does and why before showing the code.

## Filtering Low-Expressed Genes

Genes with very low or near-zero expression across all samples add statistical noise (unstable variance estimates) without adding biological information, and can even cause a per-gene t-test to fail outright when a group's values are constant. We apply the same mean-TPM filter used in Module 1 and report exactly how many genes are removed.

```{r filter-genes, echo=TRUE}
gene_mean_expr <- counts_long %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol) %>%
  summarise(mean_tpm = mean(tpm), .groups = "drop")

n_genes_before <- nrow(gene_mean_expr)
genes_to_keep  <- gene_mean_expr %>% filter(mean_tpm >= 1) %>% pull(gene_symbol)
n_genes_after  <- length(genes_to_keep)

counts_filtered <- counts_long %>%
  filter(gene_symbol %in% genes_to_keep) %>%
  mutate(log2_tpm = log2(tpm + 1))
```

```{r table-filter}
datatable(
  tibble(
    step  = c("Genes before filtering", "Genes after filtering (mean TPM >= 1)", "Genes removed"),
    genes = c(n_genes_before, n_genes_after, n_genes_before - n_genes_after)
  ),
  rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", ordering = FALSE),
  caption = "Effect of the low-expression filter."
)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Design note.** Favorable and unfavorable histology are two different groups of patients, not two samples from the same patient — there is no pairing to exploit here, unlike a tumor-vs-adjacent-normal design. We use an **unpaired, two-sample Welch t-test**, the correct choice whenever the two groups being compared are different individuals rather than matched samples from the same individual.
</div>

## Per-Gene Differential Expression Testing

For each of the `r n_genes_after` retained genes, we run a Welch two-sample t-test comparing log2(TPM + 1) between `Favorable` and `Unfavorable` histology, using `purrr::map` to apply the test gene-by-gene and `broom::tidy()` to collect the results into a single tidy table — no custom helper function is defined, only standard tidyverse verbs applied to base R's `t.test()`.

<div class="alert-info">
**Beginner note — what does `nest()` + `map()` actually do here?** `t.test()` only ever compares two groups at a time, and we have `r n_genes_after` genes to test — one t-test per gene, run automatically instead of copy-pasted `r n_genes_after` times. `nest()` splits the long table into one mini-table per gene, `map()` runs `t.test()` once on each of those mini-tables, and `tidy()` turns each test's result back into a tidy row. The pattern — **nest, map a function over each piece, tidy, unnest** — is one of the most useful in `tidyverse` for "do the same analysis once per group," and it comes up constantly beyond just t-tests.
</div>

```{r run-de-tests, echo=TRUE}
# Nest the data by gene, run a Welch t-test per gene, and tidy the results.
# possibly() guards against the rare gene where a group has zero variance,
# which would otherwise make t.test() error and stop the whole pipeline.
de_results_raw <- counts_filtered %>%
  select(gene_symbol, case_submitter_id, histologic_subtype, log2_tpm) %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol) %>%
  nest() %>%
  mutate(
    test_result = map(data, possibly(~ t.test(log2_tpm ~ histologic_subtype, data = .x), otherwise = NULL))
  )

n_tests_failed <- sum(map_lgl(de_results_raw$test_result, is.null))

de_results <- de_results_raw %>%
  filter(!map_lgl(test_result, is.null)) %>%
  mutate(tidy_result = map(test_result, tidy)) %>%
  unnest(tidy_result) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # estimate1 = mean log2 TPM in "Favorable", estimate2 = mean in "Unfavorable"
  # (t.test(formula, data) orders groups alphabetically: Favorable before Unfavorable).
  rename(mean_log2_Favorable = estimate1, mean_log2_Unfavorable = estimate2) %>%
  mutate(
    log2FC = mean_log2_Favorable - mean_log2_Unfavorable,
    p_adj  = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")
  ) %>%
  select(gene_symbol, mean_log2_Favorable, mean_log2_Unfavorable, log2FC, statistic, p.value, p_adj) %>%
  arrange(p_adj)
```

```{r table-de-summary}
datatable(
  tibble(
    category = c("Genes tested", "Genes where the test could not be run",
                 "Significant (p_adj < 0.05)", "Significant (p_adj < 0.05) and |log2FC| > 1"),
    genes    = c(nrow(de_results), n_tests_failed, sum(de_results$p_adj < 0.05),
                 sum(de_results$p_adj < 0.05 & abs(de_results$log2FC) > 1))
  ),
  rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", ordering = FALSE),
  caption = "Favorable vs Unfavorable: how many genes pass each threshold."
)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Signal size, checked rather than assumed.** The number of genes reaching `p_adj < 0.05` here is a moderate fraction of all genes tested — not the near-total-genome signal a dominant confounder (e.g. a difference in cell-type composition between groups) would typically produce. That is a reassuring, not a conclusive, sign: it still does not make any single gene a validated biomarker on its own. We inspect *what kind* of genes top the list directly below, not just how many are significant.
</div>

## Volcano Plot

A volcano plot jointly displays effect size (log2 fold-change, x-axis) and statistical significance (−log10 adjusted p-value, y-axis), making it easy to spot genes that are both strongly and confidently changed — the genes most likely to be useful, reproducible biomarkers rather than statistically significant but practically negligible changes.

```{r volcano-plot, echo=TRUE, fig.height=7}
volcano_data <- de_results %>%
  mutate(
    neg_log10_padj = -log10(p_adj),
    significance = case_when(
      p_adj < 0.05 & abs(log2FC) > 1 ~ "Significant & |log2FC| > 1",
      p_adj < 0.05                   ~ "Significant only",
      TRUE                            ~ "Not significant"
    )
  )

p_volcano <- volcano_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = log2FC, y = neg_log10_padj, color = significance, text = gene_symbol)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "Significant & |log2FC| > 1" = "#e74c3c",
    "Significant only"           = "#2980b9",
    "Not significant"            = "grey70"
  )) +
  labs(
    x = "log2 fold-change (Favorable vs Unfavorable)",
    y = "-log10(adjusted p-value)",
    title = "Volcano plot of per-gene differential expression",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

ggplotly(p_volcano, tooltip = c("text", "x", "y"))
```

## Visualizing the Result: A Heatmap of Top Candidates

A volcano plot summarizes one number per gene (its overall group difference); a heatmap shows the underlying sample-by-sample pattern behind that number, which is often the fastest way to spot whether a "significant" gene is a clean, consistent group difference or driven by just one or two outlier samples. We plot the top 30 candidates by adjusted p-value, with each gene's expression converted to a **z-score** (its values expressed as standard deviations from that gene's own mean) so that genes measured on very different expression scales can be compared side by side on one color axis.

```{r heatmap-top-genes, echo=TRUE, fig.height=9}
# Take the top 30 candidates by adjusted p-value for a readable heatmap.
top_heatmap_genes <- de_results %>% slice_head(n = 30) %>% pull(gene_symbol)

# Z-score each gene's log2 TPM across samples: this puts every gene on a
# comparable scale (mean 0, SD 1) regardless of its absolute expression level.
heatmap_data <- counts_filtered %>%
  filter(gene_symbol %in% top_heatmap_genes) %>%
  select(gene_symbol, case_submitter_id, histologic_subtype, log2_tpm) %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol) %>%
  mutate(z_score = as.numeric(scale(log2_tpm))) %>%
  ungroup()

# Order samples by histology (so the two groups appear as visually separate
# blocks) and genes by their rank in de_results (most significant at top).
sample_order <- sample_metadata %>% arrange(histologic_subtype, case_submitter_id) %>% pull(case_submitter_id)

heatmap_data <- heatmap_data %>%
  mutate(
    case_submitter_id = factor(case_submitter_id, levels = sample_order),
    gene_symbol        = factor(gene_symbol, levels = rev(top_heatmap_genes))
  )
```

```{r plot-heatmap, fig.height=9}
p_heatmap <- heatmap_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = case_submitter_id, y = gene_symbol, fill = z_score, text = paste0(gene_symbol, " / ", case_submitter_id, " (", histologic_subtype, ")"))) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2980b9", mid = "white", high = "#e74c3c", midpoint = 0) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "z-score",
       title = "Top 30 candidate biomarkers across all samples (log2 counts, per-gene z-scored)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, size = 6),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7))

ggplotly(p_heatmap, tooltip = "text")
```

<div class="alert-info">
**What to look for.** If the top candidates are genuine, consistent group markers, the heatmap should show two clearly separated blocks of color, one per group, across nearly every gene shown. Patchy patterns — a gene that looks "significant" but shows the expected color in only a handful of samples per group — are a visual early-warning sign of a result driven by outliers rather than a consistent group effect, and are worth double-checking against Module 1's PCA and correlation results before trusting them.
</div>

## Top Candidate Biomarkers

The table below lists the top 200 genes ranked by adjusted p-value (out of `r sum(de_results$p_adj < 0.05)` significant at `p_adj < 0.05`). The full result table for all `r nrow(de_results)` tested genes is exported to CSV below the table for anyone who needs the complete list.

```{r table-top-candidates}
top_candidates <- de_results %>% slice_head(n = 200)

datatable(
  top_candidates %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 4))),
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel", "pdf"), pageLength = 15),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "Top 200 candidate biomarkers ranked by adjusted p-value."
)
```

```{r export-de-results, echo=TRUE}
# Persist the full differential expression table for use in Module 3 and for
# anyone who wants the complete, unfiltered result set.
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(de_results, "results/differential_expression_results.csv")
```

## A Quick Biological Sanity Check

Before treating any of the above as a real finding, the simplest and most informative check is to just read the names of the top genes.

```{r top15-table}
top15 <- de_results %>% slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 4)))
kable(top15, caption = "Top 15 candidates by adjusted p-value.")
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Interpretation, stated plainly.** The top-ranked genes above span several different functional categories rather than one narrow theme — for example `SOX15` (a SRY-box transcription factor involved in development), `ME1` (malic enzyme, a metabolic/lipogenesis gene), `CIRBP` (a cold/stress-inducible RNA-binding protein), `GGH` (gamma-glutamyl hydrolase, folate metabolism), and `ADAMTS10` (an extracellular-matrix protease). That functional spread is itself informative: unlike a single dominant, narrowly-themed signature (which would suggest one confound driving most of the result), this list looks more consistent with a real, multi-pathway biological difference between favorable and anaplastic histology — though confirming *why* any specific gene differs would need follow-up beyond this one expression comparison.
</div>

## Adding a Real Negative Control: Tumor vs. Normal Kidney

Favorable-vs-Unfavorable is a **tumor-vs-tumor** comparison — it never asks what either subtype looks like relative to normal tissue. TARGET-WT also includes a small number of genuinely matched **normal kidney** samples from the same consortium, which lets us ask that more fundamental question directly: how does each histology subtype differ from non-cancerous tissue?

```{r load-controls, echo=TRUE}
# Real matched-normal ("Solid Tissue Normal") RNA-seq samples, assembled the
# same way as the tumor matrix (see data-prep/build_target_wt_data.R).
control_counts_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/TARGET_WT_control_gene_expression_tpm.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  rename(gene_symbol = gene_name)

control_clinical <- read_csv("data/TARGET_WT_control_clinical_raw.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Only 6 real normal samples exist for this entire project** (TARGET-WT has 652 registered cases in total, but only 6 open-access, matched-normal RNA-seq files) — and all 6 happen to come from **Favorable**-histology patients; none exist for Unfavorable. This is exactly why Module 2's main comparison (above) is tumor-vs-tumor rather than each subtype vs. its own control: there is no "Unfavorable-vs-its-own-control" comparison to run. What follows instead compares **each tumor subtype against this same shared pool of 6 normals** — a real but small, intentionally-labeled-as-small reference group.
</div>

```{r check-id-overlap, echo=TRUE}
# A real metadata subtlety worth seeing directly: all 6 normal-tissue donors
# ALSO appear among the 82 Favorable tumor samples already loaded above --
# same patient, two different biological samples (tumor + matched normal).
# case_submitter_id alone can't distinguish them, so the normal samples are
# tracked by their own sample_submitter_id (e.g. "...-11A") instead, and the
# two groups are combined explicitly in code below rather than via a join on
# case_submitter_id, which would silently fan out for these 6 shared patients.
datatable(
  control_clinical %>%
    mutate(also_has_tumor_sample = case_submitter_id %in% sample_metadata$case_submitter_id),
  rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", ordering = FALSE),
  caption = "The 6 normal-tissue samples, and whether the same patient also has a tumor sample."
)
```

```{r prep-de-vs-control, echo=TRUE}
fav_ids   <- sample_metadata %>% filter(histologic_subtype == "Favorable")   %>% pull(case_submitter_id)
unfav_ids <- sample_metadata %>% filter(histologic_subtype == "Unfavorable") %>% pull(case_submitter_id)

control_long <- control_counts_raw %>%
  pivot_longer(-gene_symbol, names_to = "sample_submitter_id", values_to = "tpm") %>%
  mutate(group = "Control")

# The same nested-t-test pipeline as above is needed twice (once per tumor
# subtype vs. the same control pool) -- a genuinely repeated, multi-step
# procedure, so it is wrapped in one function rather than duplicating the
# whole block, per the "no custom functions unless the logic is repeated and
# has no shorter tidyverse equivalent" rule.
run_de_vs_control <- function(tumor_label, tumor_ids) {
  tumor_long <- counts_raw %>%
    select(gene_symbol, all_of(tumor_ids)) %>%
    pivot_longer(-gene_symbol, names_to = "sample_submitter_id", values_to = "tpm") %>%
    mutate(group = tumor_label)

  # Factor levels are set explicitly (tumor first, Control second) so
  # t.test()'s estimate1/estimate2 always mean "tumor" / "control" --
  # alphabetical default ordering would otherwise flip this per comparison
  # ("Control" < "Favorable" but "Control" < "Unfavorable" too).
  combined <- bind_rows(tumor_long, control_long) %>%
    mutate(
      log2_tpm = log2(tpm + 1),
      group = factor(group, levels = c(tumor_label, "Control"))
    )

  genes_keep_vc <- combined %>%
    group_by(gene_symbol) %>%
    summarise(mean_tpm = mean(tpm), .groups = "drop") %>%
    filter(mean_tpm >= 1) %>%
    pull(gene_symbol)

  de_vc <- combined %>%
    filter(gene_symbol %in% genes_keep_vc) %>%
    select(gene_symbol, sample_submitter_id, group, log2_tpm) %>%
    group_by(gene_symbol) %>%
    nest() %>%
    mutate(test_result = map(data, possibly(~ t.test(log2_tpm ~ group, data = .x), otherwise = NULL))) %>%
    filter(!map_lgl(test_result, is.null)) %>%
    mutate(tidy_result = map(test_result, tidy)) %>%
    unnest(tidy_result) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    rename(mean_log2_tumor = estimate1, mean_log2_control = estimate2) %>%
    mutate(
      log2FC = mean_log2_tumor - mean_log2_control,
      p_adj  = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")
    ) %>%
    select(gene_symbol, mean_log2_tumor, mean_log2_control, log2FC, statistic, p.value, p_adj) %>%
    arrange(p_adj)

  list(genes_before = n_distinct(combined$gene_symbol), genes_after = length(genes_keep_vc), results = de_vc)
}

de_favorable_vs_control   <- run_de_vs_control("Favorable", fav_ids)
de_unfavorable_vs_control <- run_de_vs_control("Unfavorable", unfav_ids)
```

```{r table-de-vs-control}
datatable(
  tibble(
    comparison     = c("Favorable vs Control", "Unfavorable vs Control"),
    tumor_samples  = c(length(fav_ids), length(unfav_ids)),
    control_samples = ncol(control_counts_raw) - 1,
    genes_tested   = c(de_favorable_vs_control$genes_after, de_unfavorable_vs_control$genes_after),
    significant    = c(sum(de_favorable_vs_control$results$p_adj < 0.05),
                       sum(de_unfavorable_vs_control$results$p_adj < 0.05)),
    significant_and_fc = c(sum(de_favorable_vs_control$results$p_adj < 0.05 & abs(de_favorable_vs_control$results$log2FC) > 1),
                           sum(de_unfavorable_vs_control$results$p_adj < 0.05 & abs(de_unfavorable_vs_control$results$log2FC) > 1))
  ),
  rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", ordering = FALSE),
  caption = "Tumor vs normal kidney: genes tested and significant (p_adj < 0.05; significant_and_fc adds |log2FC| > 1)."
)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**A much larger signal here — and that is expected, not a red flag.** Tumor-vs-*normal* comparisons routinely show far more genes changed than tumor-vs-tumor comparisons, because tumor tissue differs from normal tissue in dozens of basic ways at once (proliferation rate, immune infiltrate, blood supply, cell-type composition) — the opposite of a confound to worry about, since that *is* the biology being measured. What matters here is whether the top genes make biological sense.
</div>

```{r top10-vs-control-tables}
kable(de_favorable_vs_control$results %>% slice_head(n = 10) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 4))),
      caption = "Top 10 genes, Favorable tumor vs normal kidney.")
kable(de_unfavorable_vs_control$results %>% slice_head(n = 10) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 4))),
      caption = "Top 10 genes, Unfavorable tumor vs normal kidney.")
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Biological sanity check.** Both lists are topped by `SIX1`, `SIX2`, and `EYA1` — three transcription factors that define the embryonic nephron progenitor program and are switched off in mature kidney, but are a textbook hallmark of Wilms tumor, which arises from retained embryonic kidney (blastemal) tissue. Seeing exactly these genes, unprompted, at the top of a real tumor-vs-normal comparison is a strong positive sanity check that this pipeline is measuring real biology.
</div>

```{r export-de-vs-control, echo=TRUE}
write_csv(de_favorable_vs_control$results, "results/differential_expression_favorable_vs_control.csv")
write_csv(de_unfavorable_vs_control$results, "results/differential_expression_unfavorable_vs_control.csv")
```

<div class="alert-info">
**What carries forward to Module 3.** The Favorable-vs-Unfavorable candidate list above stands on its own as a tumor-subtype comparison. For the network-inference step in Module 3, though, we deliberately switch to **these two vs-control lists**: genes that distinguish a subtype from normal kidney are a more principled starting panel for asking "how is regulation wired differently in this subtype" than genes that merely differ between the two tumor subtypes, which could just as easily reflect a difference in cell-of-origin rather than regulatory rewiring.
</div>

# Part 4 — Light Hands-On: Guided Exploration

Every threshold used so far (`p_adj < 0.05`, `|log2FC| > 1`) was a choice, not a law of nature. The point of this section is **not** to teach new statistics — it is to build a feel for how moving those thresholds changes what counts as a "finding," using the two sliders below. They control a live-linked plot and table (built with the `crosstalk` package): drag either slider and both update instantly, entirely in your browser, with no code to re-run.

For readability and file size, this explorer is restricted to the 300 genes already ranked most significant in `de_results` — sliding the thresholds below explores *which of these* survive stricter cutoffs, not the full `r nrow(de_results)`-gene universe.

<div class="alert-info">
**Try this, in order (≈5 min):** (1) leave both sliders at their default, and note roughly how many genes are shown; (2) drag the fold-change slider up until it reads "Minimum |log2 fold-change| = 2" and note how the point count on the plot drops; (3) put that slider back, and instead drag the p-value slider down to its minimum — compare which of the two moves removed more genes. There is no right answer; the point is to see the two thresholds behave differently.
</div>

```{r crosstalk-explorer, echo=TRUE}
# SharedData links the plot and the table below: any filter applied via the
# sliders is applied to both simultaneously, client-side, in the rendered HTML.
explorer_data <- de_results %>%
  slice_head(n = 300) %>%
  mutate(neg_log10_padj = -log10(p_adj), abs_log2FC = abs(log2FC))

shared_explorer <- SharedData$new(explorer_data, key = ~gene_symbol, group = "de_explorer")
```

```{r crosstalk-widget, fig.height=6}
bscols(
  widths = c(3, 9),
  list(
    filter_slider("fc_threshold", "Minimum |log2 fold-change|",
                   shared_explorer, ~abs_log2FC, step = 0.1, width = "100%"),
    filter_slider("padj_threshold", "Maximum adjusted p-value",
                   shared_explorer, ~p_adj, step = 0.001, width = "100%")
  ),
  plot_ly(shared_explorer, x = ~log2FC, y = ~neg_log10_padj, type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
          text = ~gene_symbol, hoverinfo = "text",
          marker = list(size = 7, opacity = 0.6, color = "#2980b9")) %>%
    layout(xaxis = list(title = "log2 fold-change (Favorable vs Unfavorable)"),
           yaxis = list(title = "-log10(adjusted p-value)"),
           title = "Drag the sliders on the left to filter this plot and the table below")
)
```

```{r crosstalk-table}
datatable(
  shared_explorer,
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel"), pageLength = 8,
                 columnDefs = list(list(visible = FALSE, targets = c(7, 8)))),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "Candidate list filtered live by the sliders above."
)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**What to try, and what to notice.** Push the fold-change slider up while leaving the p-value slider lenient, then do the reverse. Notice that the two thresholds do not always agree on which genes "matter" — a gene can be highly significant with a small effect size (common with large sample sizes) or have a large effect size that just misses significance (common with small, noisy groups). There is no universally correct combination; the right threshold depends on what the candidate list will be used for next (a shortlist for expensive follow-up validation calls for stricter cutoffs than an exploratory hypothesis-generating list).
</div>

# Part 5 — Closing Pediatric Lens

This entire analysis ran on **`r nrow(sample_metadata)` samples** (`r sum(sample_metadata$histologic_subtype == "Favorable")` favorable, `r sum(sample_metadata$histologic_subtype == "Unfavorable")` unfavorable) — and that number, by real-world pediatric-oncology standards, is actually a relatively large, hard-won cohort: it exists only because the NCI's **TARGET** program and the Children's Oncology Group coordinated a multi-institution trial (NWTS-5) specifically to assemble enough anaplastic (unfavorable-histology) cases to study at all, since that subtype is individually rare.

- **A p-value is not a biomarker.** Effect size (`log2FC`) and biological plausibility matter as much as, or more than, the adjusted p-value alone — the moderate, functionally diverse signal seen in this module is a reassuring sign, but still not sufficient on its own.
- **Pediatric rare disease and cancer studies are almost always underpowered by adult-oncology standards.** With `r sum(sample_metadata$histologic_subtype=="Unfavorable")` unfavorable-histology samples here, and adult cancer cohort studies routinely running into the hundreds or thousands, every statistical test in this module runs on a fraction of the data an equivalent adult study would have — which argues for prioritizing genes with **large, consistent effect sizes** over borderline p-values (exactly what Part 4's sliders let you feel directly), and for treating any single-cohort candidate list as hypothesis-generating rather than diagnostic.
- **Any candidate list needs independent validation** — an orthogonal cohort, an orthogonal assay (e.g. qPCR, IHC), or both — before it can be called a biomarker in the clinical sense. Statistical significance in an expression comparison is also not the same question as mechanism: Module 3 takes the natural next step by asking how the genes distinguishing each subtype from normal kidney *regulate each other differently* between Favorable and Unfavorable, using gene regulatory network inference.
